claim: Adult neural stem cells are located in discrete brain regions.
source: Adult neural stem cells, located in discrete brain regions, generate new neurons throughout life.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is part of established scientific knowledge about adult neurogenesis.

claim: Adult neural stem cells generate new neurons throughout life.
source: Adult neural stem cells, located in discrete brain regions, generate new neurons throughout life.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience presented in the abstract.

claim: Adult neural stem cells are specialized astrocytes.
source: These stem cells are specialized astrocytes, but astrocytes in other brain regions do not generate neurons under physiological conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Astrocytes in other brain regions do not generate neurons under physiological conditions.
source: These stem cells are specialized astrocytes, but astrocytes in other brain regions do not generate neurons under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about astrocyte behavior under normal conditions.

claim: Striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis in mice after stroke.
source: After stroke, however, striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis in mice, triggered by decreased Notch signaling.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript (Magnusson et al., 2014).

claim: Neurogenesis by striatal astrocytes after stroke is triggered by decreased Notch signaling.
source: After stroke, however, striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis in mice, triggered by decreased Notch signaling.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript (Magnusson et al., 2014).

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to characterize neurogenesis by Notch-depleted striatal astrocytes in vivo.
source: We used single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize neurogenesis by Notch-depleted striatal astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Striatal astrocytes were located upstream of neural stem cells in the neuronal lineage.
source: Striatal astrocytes were located upstream of neural stem cells in the neuronal lineage.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: As astrocytes initiated neurogenesis, they became transcriptionally very similar to subventricular zone stem cells.
source: As astrocytes initiated neurogenesis, they became transcriptionally very similar to subventricular zone stem cells, progressing through a near-identical neurogenic program.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptional analysis comparing striatal astrocytes to SVZ stem cells.

claim: Striatal astrocytes progress through a near-identical neurogenic program to subventricular zone stem cells.
source: As astrocytes initiated neurogenesis, they became transcriptionally very similar to subventricular zone stem cells, progressing through a near-identical neurogenic program.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative transcriptional analysis.

claim: Notch-depleted astrocytes in the non-neurogenic cortex initiated neurogenesis.
source: Surprisingly, in the non-neurogenic cortex, Notch-depleted astrocytes also initiated neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of cortical astrocytes.

claim: Cortical astrocytes and many striatal astrocytes stalled before entering transit-amplifying divisions.
source: Yet, these cortical astrocytes, and many striatal ones, stalled before entering transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Infusion of epidermal growth factor enabled stalled striatal astrocytes to resume neurogenesis.
source: Infusion of epidermal growth factor enabled stalled striatal astrocytes to resume neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the EGF injection experiments.

claim: Parenchymal astrocytes are latent neural stem cells.
source: We conclude that parenchymal astrocytes are latent neural stem cells and that targeted interventions can guide them through their neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Targeted interventions can guide parenchymal astrocytes through their neuronal differentiation.
source: We conclude that parenchymal astrocytes are latent neural stem cells and that targeted interventions can guide them through their neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the EGF injection experiments.

claim: Neurogenesis is extremely limited in the adult brain.
source: Neurogenesis is extremely limited in the adult brain.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: In most mammals, specialized astrocytes in the subventricular zone and hippocampal dentate gyrus are stem cells and generate new neurons continuously.
source: In most mammals, specialized astrocytes in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) are stem cells and generate new neurons continuously, but apart from that, the brain's ability to replace lost neurons is very limited.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult neurogenesis.

claim: Apart from the SVZ and DG, the brain's ability to replace lost neurons is very limited.
source: In most mammals, specialized astrocytes in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) are stem cells and generate new neurons continuously, but apart from that, the brain's ability to replace lost neurons is very limited.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limited regenerative capacity of the adult brain.

claim: Some astrocytes in the mouse striatum can generate neurons in response to an experimental stroke or excitotoxic lesion.
source: However, in response to an experimental stroke or excitotoxic lesion, some astrocytes in the mouse striatum can generate neurons (Magnusson et al., 2014; Nato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neurogenic response of striatal astrocytes is regulated by Notch signaling.
source: This neurogenic response is regulated by Notch signaling and can be activated even in the uninjured mouse striatum by deleting the Notch-mediating transcription factor Rbpj (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neurogenesis by striatal astrocytes can be activated in the uninjured mouse striatum by deleting Rbpj.
source: This neurogenic response is regulated by Notch signaling and can be activated even in the uninjured mouse striatum by deleting the Notch-mediating transcription factor Rbpj (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis by passing through a transit-amplifying cell stage.
source: Striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis by passing through a transit-amplifying cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Astrocytes make up 10-20% of all brain cells in mice.
source: Astrocytes make up a large fraction of all brain cells (10–20% in mice) (Sun et al., 2017) and are distributed throughout the central nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Astrocytes are distributed throughout the central nervous system.
source: Astrocytes make up a large fraction of all brain cells (10–20% in mice) (Sun et al., 2017) and are distributed throughout the central nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about astrocyte distribution.

claim: Injury-induced neurogenesis by astrocytes occurs almost exclusively in the striatum.
source: Although certain injuries and Rbpj deletion can both trigger neurogenesis by astrocytes, it almost exclusively does so in the striatum.
evidence: This is based on prior observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Primarily astrocytes in the medial striatum readily activate neurogenic properties.
source: And even within the striatum, primarily the astrocytes in the medial striatum readily activate neurogenic properties (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Deletion of Rbpj activates a latent neurogenic program in striatal astrocytes.
source: Deletion of the gene encoding the Notch-mediating transcription factor Rbpj activates a latent neurogenic program in striatal astrocytes (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and is a key finding of the current study.

claim: Not all striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis after Rbpj deletion.
source: Not all striatal astrocytes undergo neurogenesis, shown by the restricted distribution of Dcx+ neuroblasts and the fact that many recombined astrocytes (gray) remain even 2 months after Rbpj deletion.
evidence: This is based on observations from the study shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The AAV-Cre dataset contains astrocytes and their neurogenic progeny, along with cells from the oligodendroglial lineage and microglia.
source: This sample encompasses astrocytes and their neurogenic progeny, along with cells from the oligodendroglial lineage, and microglia.
evidence: This describes the composition of the AAV-Cre dataset as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is possible to use single-cell RNA sequencing to study the transcriptional mechanisms underlying the astrocyte neurogenic program.
source: We conclude that it is possible to use single-cell RNA sequencing to study the transcriptional mechanisms underlying the astrocyte neurogenic program.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the successful reconstruction of the neurogenic trajectory using the AAV-Cre dataset.

claim: Two weeks after Rbpj deletion, astrocytes had upregulated genes mostly related to transcription, translation and metabolism.
source: Two weeks after Rbpj deletion, astrocytes had upregulated genes mostly related to transcription, translation and metabolism (Figure 2b, S1g, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Neurogenesis by parenchymal astrocytes involves transit-amplifying divisions and does not occur through direct transdifferentiation.
source: This analysis confirmed the previous finding that neurogenesis by parenchymal astrocytes involves transit-amplifying divisions (Magnusson et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2013), and does not occur through direct transdifferentiation, a process during which intermediate stages of differentiation are skipped (Briggs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is confirmed by the pseudotemporal analysis and supported by prior research.

claim: As astrocytes initiate neurogenesis, genes associated with lipid and carbohydrate metabolism are at first upregulated but dramatically downregulated as cells enter transit-amplifying divisions.
source: We found that, as astrocytes initiated their neurogenic program, genes associated with metabolism, particularly lipid (e.g. Fabp5, Fasn, Elovl5) and carbohydrate metabolism (e.g. Gapdh, Aldoa, Aldoc) were at first upregulated but dramatically downregulated as cells entered transit-amplifying divisions (Figure 2e–f, [Cluster 1]).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene clustering analysis shown in Figure 2e-f.

claim: The neurogenic program requires high metabolic activity to prepare for transit-amplifying divisions.
source: This suggested that the neurogenic program requires high metabolic activity to prepare for transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed upregulation of metabolic genes before transit-amplifying divisions.

claim: The expression of genes involved in the regulation of transcription and translation progressively increases throughout the neurogenic process.
source: In addition to these metabolic genes, the expression of genes involved in the regulation of transcription (e.g. mRNA splicing genes Snrpb, Srsf5, Srsf3) and translation (e.g. ribosomal subunits Rpl17, Rpl23, Rps11) progressively increased throughout the neurogenic process (Figure 2e–f, [Cluster 2]).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene clustering analysis shown in Figure 2e-f.

claim: The number of genes detected per cell increases in the initial stages of neurogenesis.
source: Accordingly, we found that the number of genes detected per cell increased in the initial stages of neurogenesis (Figure 2g): pre-division astrocytes expressed 1.4 times as many genes as ground-state astrocytes (p=10−12; 95% C.I. 1.3–1.5; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Pre-division astrocytes expressed 1.4 times as many genes as ground-state astrocytes.
source: pre-division astrocytes expressed 1.4 times as many genes as ground-state astrocytes (p=10−12; 95% C.I. 1.3–1.5; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance.

claim: No cell size increase was observed during the early phase of neurogenesis.
source: In theory, such an increase in the number of detected genes could be an artifact caused by a simultaneous increase in cell size; however, no cell size increase was observed during this early phase of neurogenesis, as measured by flow cytometer forward scatter (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Synapse maintenance is compromised very early as astrocytes initiate neurogenesis.
source: This suggested that synapse maintenance was compromised very early as astrocytes initiated neurogenesis, but also that some of the same genes are important for synapse maintenance in both astrocytes and neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed downregulation of synapse-associated genes.

claim: Some genes are important for synapse maintenance in both astrocytes and neurons.
source: This suggested that synapse maintenance was compromised very early as astrocytes initiated neurogenesis, but also that some of the same genes are important for synapse maintenance in both astrocytes and neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of gene expression showing initial downregulation followed by upregulation in neuroblasts.

claim: Throughout the initial phase of neurogenesis and up until the point where cells entered transit-amplifying divisions, astrocytes maintained normal astrocyte morphology and expression of common marker genes.
source: Throughout the initial phase of neurogenesis and up until the point where cells entered transit-amplifying divisions, astrocytes maintained normal astrocyte morphology and expression of common marker genes (e.g. Aqp4, S100b, Slc1a2 [Glt1], Glul) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b–c, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b-c and Video 1.

claim: Neurogenic astrocytes never showed signs of reactive gliosis.
source: They never showed signs of reactive gliosis (e.g. morphological changes or upregulation of Gfap), indicating that reactive gliosis is not required for neurogenesis by astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is an observation from the study with an inference about the independence of neurogenesis from reactive gliosis.

claim: Reactive gliosis is not required for neurogenesis by astrocytes in vivo.
source: They never showed signs of reactive gliosis (e.g. morphological changes or upregulation of Gfap), indicating that reactive gliosis is not required for neurogenesis by astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that neurogenic astrocytes do not show signs of reactive gliosis.

claim: Astrocytes lose their typical branched morphology gradually, only after entering transit-amplifying divisions.
source: As the astrocytes entered the neurogenic program, they did eventually lose their typical branched morphology; however, they did so only gradually, and only after entering transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c and Video 1.

claim: Many clustered transit-amplifying cells retained trace levels of the astrocyte marker protein S100β.
source: As an additional sign that they originated from parenchymal astrocytes, many clustered transit-amplifying cells retained trace levels of the astrocyte marker protein S100β, even though they no longer expressed the S100b gene.
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3d-g.

claim: S100β protein is found in parenchymal astrocytes but not in SVZ stem cells.
source: S100β protein is found in parenchymal astrocytes but not in SVZ stem cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d–g).
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3d-g.

claim: Many quiescent neural stem cells in Drosophila melanogaster are halted in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: A recent study in Drosophila melanogaster showed that many quiescent neural stem cells are halted in the G2 phase of the cell cycle (Otsuki and Brand, 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research in Drosophila.

claim: Some single striatal astrocytes that had not yet divided were EdU+, suggesting they initiated the cell cycle by synthesizing DNA.
source: However, we analyzed EdU incorporation in dividing striatal astrocytes. We found some single astrocytes that had not yet divided but were EdU+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c). This suggested that these astrocytes initiated the cell cycle by synthesizing DNA and thus had not been suspended in the G2 phase.
evidence: This is a finding from EdU incorporation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Striatal astrocytes had not been suspended in the G2 phase.
source: This suggested that these astrocytes initiated the cell cycle by synthesizing DNA and thus had not been suspended in the G2 phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EdU incorporation data.

claim: The striatal astrocytes and their progeny clustered closely together with the corresponding stages of SVZ cells.
source: A UMAP analysis of these cells together with our AAV-Cre dataset revealed that the striatal astrocytes and their progeny clustered closely together with the corresponding stages of SVZ cells (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is a finding from the integrated UMAP analysis shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Neurogenesis in the striatum and SVZ proceeds through the same general developmental stages.
source: This indicated that neurogenesis in these two brain regions proceeds through the same general developmental stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: Astrocyte Cluster 2 grouped closely together with SVZ neural stem cells, indicating that these cells are transcriptionally similar.
source: Particularly interesting was the observation that our 'Astrocyte Cluster 2' grouped closely together with SVZ neural stem cells (Figure 3b), indicating that these cells are transcriptionally similar.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ground state astrocytes were located upstream of the SVZ stem cells on the neurogenic trajectory.
source: Interestingly, on this neurogenic trajectory, ground state astrocytes were located upstream of the SVZ stem cells, as if representing highly quiescent cells that pass through an initial activation phase before joining the SVZ stem cells (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotemporal analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: SVZ neural stem cells appear to be maintained at a high baseline level of metabolic gene expression.
source: Intriguingly, however, whereas SVZ neural stem cells appear to be maintained at a high baseline level of metabolic gene expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c), striatal astrocytes first passed through a phase of metabolic gene upregulation to reach this level, seen by superimposing the striatum-only (Figure 2e) and SVZ-only (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) metabolic gene curves (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Striatal astrocytes first pass through a phase of metabolic gene upregulation to reach the level of SVZ stem cells.
source: Intriguingly, however, whereas SVZ neural stem cells appear to be maintained at a high baseline level of metabolic gene expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c), striatal astrocytes first passed through a phase of metabolic gene upregulation to reach this level, seen by superimposing the striatum-only (Figure 2e) and SVZ-only (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) metabolic gene curves (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing metabolic gene expression patterns shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The neurogenic program in striatal astrocytes starts with an activation phase during which these astrocytes begin to resemble SVZ stem cells with regard to metabolism-associated genes.
source: This suggested that the neurogenic program in striatal astrocytes starts with an activation phase during which these astrocytes begin to resemble SVZ stem cells with regard to metabolism-associated genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic gene expression patterns.

claim: There is a 1.7-times difference in the number of genes detected between adult SVZ stem cells and striatal astrocytes.
source: This difference is similar in magnitude to a previously detected 1.7-times difference between adult SVZ stem cells and striatal astrocytes (Gokce et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research.

claim: The gene expression activity of Rbpj-deficient astrocytes begins to quantitatively resemble that of neural stem cells.
source: This suggested that the gene expression activity of Rbpj-deficient astrocytes began to quantitatively resemble that of neural stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of gene detection numbers.

claim: Signaling entropy is a measure of the interconnectedness of a cell's proteome.
source: 'Signaling entropy' is a measure of the interconnectedness of a cell's proteome. It represents the average number of possible protein-protein interactions by all proteins expressed by a cell.
evidence: This is a definition of the signaling entropy concept.

claim: Signaling entropy is a reliable proxy for a cell's differentiation potency.
source: It is a reliable proxy for a cell's differentiation potency (Teschendorff and Enver, 2017; Chen and Teschendorff, 2019), the underlying rationale being that a highly interacting proteome enables promiscuous signaling, which in turn facilitates responding to a variety of differentiation signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SVZ cells exhibit their maximum signaling entropy as activated stem cells or transit-amplifying cells.
source: As a validation of the signaling entropy concept, we plotted signaling entropy versus pseudotime in the SVZ dataset and saw that SVZ cells exhibit their maximum signaling entropy as activated stem cells or transit-amplifying cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a finding from the signaling entropy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The signaling entropy of striatal astrocytes increased after Rbpj deletion to the levels seen in SVZ stem cells.
source: We found that the signaling entropy of striatal astrocytes increased after Rbpj deletion (Figure 3f), to the levels seen in SVZ stem cells (Figure 3g) (One-way ANOVA: F = 35.62, p<0.0001; Ground-state [0.8467 ± 0.0214] vs. pre-division astrocytes [0.8771 ± 0.0171, mean ±S.D], p<0.0001 [unpaired t-test]; pre-division astrocytes vs. pre-division SVZ [0.8848 ± 0.0232], p=0.0721).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the signaling entropy analysis shown in Figure 3f-g.

claim: Striatal astrocytes achieve the same level of differentiation potency as SVZ neural stem cells.
source: This supported the conclusion that striatal astrocytes achieve the same level of differentiation potency as SVZ neural stem cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling entropy analysis.

claim: Right before entering transit-amplifying divisions, astrocytes were in their most neural stem cell-like state.
source: Right before entering transit-amplifying divisions, astrocytes were in their most neural stem cell-like state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including signaling entropy and marker gene expression.

claim: Striatal astrocytes in the pre-division state had upregulated some marker genes of neural stem cells.
source: In addition to the similarities described above, striatal astrocytes in this pre-division state had upregulated some marker genes of neural stem cells (e.g. Fabp7 [Blbp], Egfr, Ascl1, Cd9, Cd81, Slc1a3 [Glast]; Figure 3h and Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Some neural stem cell markers were already expressed by ground-state astrocytes and their RNA levels did not change after Rbpj deletion.
source: Other such markers were already expressed by ground-state astrocytes and their RNA levels did not change after Rbpj deletion (e.g. Tnfrsf19 (Troy), Sox2, Nr2e1 (Tlx), Msi1 [Musashi-1], Rarres2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Some classical neural stem cell markers were never upregulated by Rbpj-deficient astrocytes.
source: Interestingly, some classical neural stem cell markers were never upregulated by Rbpj-deficient astrocytes. For example, Gfap, Prom1, Thbs4 and Vim remained at low levels throughout the neurogenic process (Figure 3i), showing that neurogenic astrocytes do not become transcriptionally identical to SVZ stem cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Neurogenic astrocytes do not become transcriptionally identical to SVZ stem cells.
source: For example, Gfap, Prom1, Thbs4 and Vim remained at low levels throughout the neurogenic process (Figure 3i), showing that neurogenic astrocytes do not become transcriptionally identical to SVZ stem cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that some SVZ markers are not upregulated in striatal astrocytes.

claim: Cells clustered together with other cells of the same maturational stage, regardless of which brain region they came from.
source: A clustering analysis revealed that cells clustered together with other cells of the same maturational stage, regardless of which brain region they came from (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from the integrated clustering analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Neurogenesis proceeds along the same general steps in the striatum, SVZ, and DG.
source: This indicates that neurogenesis proceeds along the same general steps in all three regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: The transcriptomes of striatal cells were more similar to those of SVZ stem cells than to those of DG stem cells in every maturational stage.
source: We found that the transcriptomes of the striatal cells were more similar to those of SVZ stem cells than to those of DG stem cells in every maturational stage, in particular at the transit-amplifying cell and neuroblast stages (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is a finding from the pairwise correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: The close transcriptional similarity between striatal and SVZ neuroblasts suggests that striatal astrocytes and SVZ stem cells are predisposed to generate very similar neuronal subtypes.
source: This revealed the close transcriptional similarity between striatal and SVZ neuroblasts, suggesting that striatal astrocytes and SVZ stem cells are predisposed to generate very similar neuronal subtypes (GABAergic interneurons), different from those in the DG (excitatory granule neurons).
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcription factor analysis of neuroblasts.

claim: The transcriptional program governing neurogenesis by striatal astrocytes is highly similar, but not identical, to that of SVZ cells.
source: In summary, the transcriptional program governing neurogenesis by striatal astrocytes is highly similar, but not identical, to that of SVZ cells, and less similar to that of DG stem cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative analyses.

claim: The similarity between striatal and SVZ neurogenic programs likely reflects a shared developmental history.
source: We speculate that this similarity likely reflects a shared developmental history.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for the observed similarity.

claim: The region-specific transcriptional signature among astrocytes is conserved when astrocytes are reprogrammed directly into neurons.
source: It has, for example, been shown that the region-specific transcriptional signature among astrocytes is conserved when astrocytes are reprogrammed directly into neurons (Herrero-navarro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research supporting the speculation.

claim: Rbpj deletion triggers astrocyte neurogenesis in layer 1 of the medial cortex.
source: We previously found that, in addition to the striatum, Rbpj deletion triggers astrocyte neurogenesis in layer 1 of the medial cortex (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Many astrocytes throughout the brain had upregulated low levels of Ascl1 in response to Rbpj deletion.
source: Intriguingly, this showed that many astrocytes throughout the brain had upregulated low levels of Ascl1 in response to Rbpj deletion (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5a-c.

claim: Astrocytes in all brain regions initiate at least one early step in a neurogenic program in response to Rbpj deletion.
source: This suggested that astrocytes in all brain regions initiate at least one early step in a neurogenic program in response to Rbpj deletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the widespread Ascl1 upregulation.

claim: All cortical astrocytes halted their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions.
source: We used Monocle to arrange the cortical cells in pseudotime together with the striatal cells and found that, regardless of brain region, cells from the different time points scored similarly along the initial stages of this pseudotime axis. However, all the cortical astrocytes halted their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotemporal analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Two weeks after Rbpj deletion, cortical astrocytes had upregulated genes mainly associated with metabolism and gene expression, just like striatal astrocytes.
source: Two weeks after Rbpj deletion, cortical astrocytes had upregulated genes mainly associated with metabolism and gene expression, just like striatal astrocytes (Figure 5g, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Cortical astrocytes steadily increased gene expression activity after Rbpj deletion.
source: They also steadily increased gene expression activity (Figure 5h), again similar to striatal cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Signaling entropy continuously increased in cortical astrocytes after Rbpj deletion to almost the same level as in striatal Rbpj-deficient astrocytes.
source: In addition, signaling entropy continuously increased after Rbpj deletion (0.85 ± 0.018 vs. 0.87 ± 0.018 [mean ± S.D.] in ground-state vs. pre-division astrocytes, respectively [p<0.0001, unpaired t test]; Figure 5i–j) to almost the same level as in the striatal Rbpj-deficient astrocytes (Figure 5j; pre-division striatal vs. cortical astrocytes: p=0.0091), suggesting that, like the striatal astrocytes, the cortical ones were shifting toward a more stem cell-like state.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the signaling entropy analysis shown in Figure 5i-j.

claim: Cortical astrocytes were shifting toward a more stem cell-like state after Rbpj deletion.
source: suggesting that, like the striatal astrocytes, the cortical ones were shifting toward a more stem cell-like state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the signaling entropy analysis.

claim: At their highest pseudotime score, cortical astrocytes were at their most stem cell-like state, characterized by upregulation of neural stem cell genes to the same RNA levels as in striatal astrocytes or SVZ stem cells.
source: At their highest pseudotime score, cortical astrocytes were at their most stem cell-like state, characterized by upregulation of neural stem cell genes such as Ascl1, Egfr, Fabp7, Pou3f4, Msi1, Slc1a3, Cd81 to the same RNA levels as in striatal astrocytes or SVZ stem cells (Figure 5k and Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5k.

claim: Cortical astrocytes were preparing to activate the full neurogenic program but were unable to enter transit-amplifying divisions.
source: Taken together, it seemed as if cortical astrocytes were preparing to activate the full neurogenic program but that they were unable to enter transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cortical astrocytes upregulate stem cell markers but do not enter transit-amplifying divisions.

claim: Cortical astrocytes can be isolated from an injury site and generate neurospheres in vitro.
source: Cortical astrocytes can be isolated from an injury site and generate neurospheres in vitro (Shimada et al., 2012; Buffo et al., 2008; Sirko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: More transplanted neural progenitor cells developed into Dcx+ neuroblasts and NeuN+ neurons in the striatum than in the cortex.
source: When the recipient mice were sacrificed and analyzed 4 weeks later, we found that more of the transplanted cells had developed into Dcx+ neuroblasts (Figure 5m) and NeuN+ neurons (Figure 5n) in the striatum than in the cortex (Dcx: striatum 52 ± 21%, cortex 20 ± 22%, mean ± S.D.; NeuN: striatum 10 ± 9%, cortex 2 ± 3%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the transplantation experiments shown in Figure 5m-n.

claim: The cortex has an environment less permissive to neurogenesis than the striatum.
source: This suggested that the cortex has an environment less permissive to neurogenesis than the striatum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transplantation experiment results.

claim: A hostile environment may help explain why Rbpj-deficient astrocytes in the cortex fail to complete the neurogenic program that they initiate.
source: Such a hostile environment may help explain why Rbpj-deficient astrocytes in the cortex fail to complete the neurogenic program that they initiate.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the transplantation results.

claim: An aborted neurogenic program may occur throughout the entire brain in response to Rbpj deletion.
source: Although we focused our analysis on the somatosensory cortex, our immunohistochemical staining of Ascl1 (Figure 5b) suggests that an aborted neurogenic program may occur throughout the entire brain in response to Rbpj deletion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the widespread Ascl1 staining shown in Figure 5b.

claim: It takes approximately 3-4 weeks until the first striatal astrocytes enter transit-amplifying divisions after Rbpj deletion.
source: We noted that, after Rbpj deletion, it takes approximately 3–4 weeks until the first striatal astrocytes enter transit-amplifying divisions (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an observation from the pseudotemporal analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Many cells isolated even 8 weeks after Rbpj deletion remained as astrocytes that seemed to have halted their development immediately prior to the transit-amplifying cell stage.
source: Yet, many cells isolated even 8 weeks after Rbpj deletion remained as astrocytes that seemed to have halted their development immediately prior to the transit-amplifying cell stage (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an observation from the pseudotemporal analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Striatal astrocytes upregulate Egfr in response to Rbpj deletion.
source: Striatal astrocytes upregulate Egfr in response to Rbpj deletion (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: EGF injection into the lateral striatum of Rbpjwt/fl control mice did not induce striatal neurogenesis.
source: In Rbpjwt/fl control mice, EGF injection on its own was not enough to induce striatal neurogenesis; neither did it induce any neuroblast migration from the SVZ (Figure 6b,d) or any detectable increase in the amount of SVZ neuroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is a finding from the EGF injection experiments shown in Figure 6b,d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: In wild-type mice, EGF did not trigger cell divisions in striatal astrocytes or non-astrocytes.
source: In wild-type mice, EGF did not trigger cell divisions in striatal astrocytes or non-astrocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a finding from the proliferation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: EGF injection into the lateral striatum did not perturb SVZ neurogenesis or trigger confounding striatal proliferation.
source: We concluded that EGF injection into the lateral striatum did not perturb SVZ neurogenesis or trigger confounding striatal proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control experiments.

claim: EGF injection into the striatum of Rbpjfl/fl mice led to a doubling in the number of reporter-positive neuroblasts compared to the vehicle-injected contralateral striatum.
source: Interestingly, however, EGF injection into the striatum of Rbpjfl/fl mice did lead to a doubling in the number of reporter-positive neuroblasts compared to the vehicle-injected contralateral striatum (216 ± 90 [EGF hemisphere, mean ± S.D.], 110 ± 61 [vehicle hemisphere]; p=0.023 [paired t-test]; Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the EGF injection experiments shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: The increase in neuroblasts after EGF injection was the result of an increased number of astrocytes entering transit-amplifying divisions rather than increased proliferation by the same number of astrocytes.
source: This increase was the result of an increased number of astrocytes entering transit-amplifying divisions rather than increased proliferation by the same number of astrocytes: EGF-injected striata contained on average twice as many neuroblast clusters as vehicle-injected striata (21 ± 10 [EGF hemisphere, mean ±S.D.], 8 ± 5 [vehicle hemisphere]; p=0.049 [paired t-test]; Figure 6e), but cluster size did not differ (p=0.59 [Mann-Whitney test]; Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: EGF administration can enable stalled neurogenic astrocytes in the striatum to initiate transit-amplifying divisions and resume neurogenesis.
source: Our results demonstrate that EGF administration can enable stalled neurogenic astrocytes in the striatum to initiate transit-amplifying divisions and resume neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EGF injection experiments.

claim: EGF exposure in the somatosensory cortex was not sufficient to make stalled Rbpj-deficient astrocytes enter transit-amplifying divisions.
source: EGF exposure in the somatosensory cortex was not sufficient to make stalled Rbpj-deficient astrocytes enter transit-amplifying divisions there (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the cortical EGF injection experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The mere act of inserting a thin syringe needle was enough of a stimulus to make some stalled cortical astrocytes enter transit-amplifying divisions.
source: Interestingly, however, the mere act of inserting a thin syringe needle was enough of a stimulus to do so in some stalled cortical astrocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the cortical injection experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: It is possible to enhance and modulate the astrocyte neurogenic program through targeted interventions.
source: Taken together, these results show that it is possible to enhance and modulate the astrocyte neurogenic program through targeted interventions, an observation that should be useful when attempting to recruit astrocytes as a reservoir for new neurons throughout the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EGF injection experiments.

claim: The brain has almost no capacity to replace lost neurons on its own.
source: The brain has almost no capacity to replace lost neurons on its own.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about brain regeneration.

claim: It is not feasible to use the SVZ and DG as sources of replacement neurons for the rest of the brain.
source: Although the SVZ and DG do contain neural stem cells, it is not feasible to use these regions as sources of replacement neurons for the rest of the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of using SVZ and DG stem cells for brain repair.

claim: Neurons generated in the SVZ or DG would need to migrate unfeasibly far to reach distant injury sites in the human brain.
source: That is mainly because neurons generated in the SVZ or DG would need to migrate unfeasibly far to reach distant injury sites in the human brain.
evidence: This is a reasoning about the practical limitations of using SVZ/DG stem cells.

claim: Astrocytes have an intrinsic neurogenic potential.
source: Astrocytes could be such a reservoir for new neurons because they have an intrinsic neurogenic potential and are very abundant.
evidence: This is supported by the findings of the study and prior research.

claim: The neurogenic program of parenchymal astrocytes is almost identical to that of SVZ neural stem cells.
source: Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to study the transcriptional program of parenchymal astrocytes as they initiate neurogenesis in response to deletion of the Notch-mediating transcription factor Rbpj. We find that the neurogenic program of parenchymal astrocytes is almost identical to that of SVZ neural stem cells.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on the comparative transcriptional analysis.

claim: Parenchymal astrocytes can be viewed as highly quiescent neural stem cells that, upon Rbpj deletion, activate a neurogenic program very similar to that of SVZ stem cells.
source: Based on the analyses in this study, we propose a model where parenchymal astrocytes are regarded as latent neural stem cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conceptual model proposed based on the study's findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Striatal astrocytes retain their distinct astrocyte morphology partly even after initiation of transit-amplifying divisions.
source: Their distinct astrocyte morphology is partly retained even after initiation of transit-amplifying divisions (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3c and Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c and Video 1.

claim: S100β protein lingers at low levels in astrocyte-derived transit-amplifying cells even when the S100b gene is no longer expressed, acting as a short-term lineage tracing marker.
source: Furthermore, S100β protein is found in many parenchymal astrocytes, but not in SVZ stem cells, and lingers at low levels in astrocyte-derived transit-amplifying cells even when the S100b gene is no longer expressed (dashed line), acting as a short-term lineage tracing marker.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3d-g and used in Figure 6i.

claim: Markers of reactive astrogliosis, such as Gfap, are upregulated in neurogenic striatal astrocytes after stroke.
source: although markers of reactive astrogliosis, such as Gfap, are upregulated in neurogenic striatal astrocytes after stroke (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research noting a difference between Rbpj deletion and stroke-induced neurogenesis.

claim: All astrocytes in the somatosensory cortex halt their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions after Rbpj deletion.
source: Astrocytes all over the brain initiate the neurogenic program in response to Rbpj deletion, but all astrocytes in the somatosensory cortex, and many in the striatum, halt their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the analysis of cortical and striatal astrocytes.

claim: Many striatal astrocytes halt their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions after Rbpj deletion.
source: Astrocytes all over the brain initiate the neurogenic program in response to Rbpj deletion, but all astrocytes in the somatosensory cortex, and many in the striatum, halt their development prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the analysis of striatal astrocytes.

claim: In the striatum, stalled astrocytes can resume neurogenesis if exposed to EGF.
source: In the striatum, stalled astrocytes can resume neurogenesis if exposed to EGF.
evidence: This is a finding from the EGF injection experiments.

claim: Initiation of the neurogenic program in astrocytes is dominated by a steady upregulation of genes associated with transcription and translation, as well as a transient wave of metabolism-associated genes.
source: Specifically, we find that initiation of the neurogenic program in astrocytes is dominated by a steady upregulation of genes associated with transcription and translation, as well as a transient wave of metabolism-associated genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene clustering analysis.

claim: Expression levels of genes associated with transcription and translation steadily increase throughout the neurogenic program in the DG and SVZ.
source: These findings fit well with what is known about neural stem cell activation in the DG and SVZ, where expression levels of genes associated with transcription and translation steadily increase throughout the neurogenic program (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parenchymal astrocytes start off at an even lower baseline level of gene expression than neural stem cells.
source: Our data suggest that parenchymal astrocytes start off at an even lower baseline level of gene expression than neural stem cells, and that they have increased the number of expressed genes ~ 1.4 fold by the time they reach their most stem cell-like state, prior to transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression analysis.

claim: The rapid burst of cell divisions is the most metabolically demanding step of the neurogenic program.
source: Metabolic gene expression peaked right before striatal astrocytes entered transit-amplifying divisions, suggesting that the rapid burst of cell divisions is the most metabolically demanding step of the neurogenic program.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of metabolic gene expression peaks.

claim: Exit from quiescence in the DG requires increased lipid metabolism.
source: In the DG, exit from quiescence requires increased lipid metabolism (Knobloch et al., 2013), and once activated stem cells enter transit-amplifying divisions, metabolic genes are downregulated, both in the DG and SVZ (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural stem cells in the DG and SVZ experience a metabolic peak prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions.
source: This similarity suggests that, like parenchymal astrocytes, neural stem cells in the DG and SVZ experience a metabolic peak prior to entering transit-amplifying divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of metabolic gene expression patterns.

claim: The most time-consuming portion of the astrocyte neurogenic program is the initial exit from deep quiescence.
source: We find that it takes 2–4 weeks for astrocytes to reach this pre-division state. One possible interpretation of this is that the most time-consuming portion of the astrocyte neurogenic program is the initial exit from deep quiescence, as is the case in quiescent muscle stem cells (Siegel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed timing and comparison to muscle stem cells.

claim: Rbpj protein may remain bound at its target promoters long after the Rbpj gene has been deleted.
source: Another (and compatible) interpretation is that Rbpj protein may remain bound at its target promoters long after the Rbpj gene has been deleted, and that the neurogenic program is initiated only when the protein level has fallen below a certain threshold.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of Rbpj deletion effects.

claim: Stable transcription factor-DNA interaction is a mechanism by which some transcription factors buffer against fluctuating transcription levels.
source: Such stable transcription factor-DNA interaction is a mechanism by which some transcription factors buffer against fluctuating transcription levels (Traets et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: All astrocytes in the striatum and somatosensory cortex are latent neural stem cells.
source: This suggests that all astrocytes in the striatum and somatosensory cortex, and perhaps in other regions as well, are latent neural stem cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that all astrocytes initiate the neurogenic program.

claim: The inability of most astrocytes to enter transit-amplifying divisions is due to a lack of proper environmental signals rather than an intrinsic inability.
source: We hypothesize that the inability of most astrocytes to enter transit-amplifying divisions is due to a lack of proper environmental signals rather than an intrinsic inability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: Parenchymal astrocytes isolated from the injured mouse cortex can generate neurospheres in vitro.
source: A large body of literature has demonstrated that parenchymal astrocytes isolated from the injured mouse cortex can generate neurospheres in vitro (Shimada et al., 2012; Buffo et al., 2008; Sirko et al., 2013), proving that astrocytes have intrinsic neural stem cell potential but lack the proper in vivo environment to realize this potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Extracellular signals can bolster and improve the astrocyte neurogenic program.
source: A single injection of EGF into the striatum was enough to make some astrocytes, which had stalled in a pre-division state, enter transit-amplifying divisions (Figure 6), showing that extracellular signals can bolster and improve the astrocyte neurogenic program.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EGF injection experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most astrocyte-derived transit-amplifying cells and neuroblasts appear in the medial striatum, close to the SVZ, in Cx30-CreER; Rbpjfl/fl mice.
source: In Cx30-CreER; Rbpjfl/fl mice, most astrocyte-derived transit-amplifying cells and neuroblasts appear in the medial striatum, close to the SVZ.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The nearby SVZ may provide a gradient of neurogenic factors into the medial striatum and establish a more permissive environment there.
source: It is possible that the nearby SVZ provides a gradient of neurogenic factors into the medial striatum and establishes a more permissive environment there. Such a gradient has indeed been shown to appear if growth factors are infused into the lateral ventricle (Yan et al., 1994; Anderson et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rbpj deletion is a biologically relevant way to activate the astrocyte neurogenic program without triggering confounding tissue processes that occur in response to injury.
source: Decreased Notch signaling is the mechanism that triggers neurogenesis by striatal astrocytes in stroke-injured mice (Magnusson et al., 2014). Therefore, the Rbpj deletion model is a biologically relevant way to activate the astrocyte neurogenic program without triggering confounding tissue processes that occur in response to injury, such as inflammation and reactive astrogliosis.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental approach based on prior research.

claim: The astrocyte neurogenic program is not dependent on simultaneous reactive gliosis.
source: Indeed, the precision afforded by our Rbpj deletion model allowed us to observe here that the astrocyte neurogenic program is not dependent on simultaneous reactive gliosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that neurogenic astrocytes do not show reactive gliosis.

claim: Neurogenesis and reactive astrogliosis are likely controlled by two independent, but compatible, transcriptional programs.
source: Instead, neurogenesis and reactive astrogliosis are likely controlled by two independent, but compatible, transcriptional programs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that neurogenesis can occur without reactive gliosis.

claim: Astrocytes in different brain regions likely use different mechanisms to lock their astrocyte identity in place.
source: It is likely that astrocytes in different brain regions use different mechanisms to lock their astrocyte identity in place.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed regional differences in neurogenic capacity.

claim: It is feasible to identify mechanisms that lock astrocyte identity and seek to target them for enhancing neurogenesis by astrocytes throughout the central nervous system.
source: Our study demonstrates that it is feasible to identify such mechanisms and seek to target them for enhancing neurogenesis by astrocytes throughout the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the study.

claim: Cx30-mediated recombination targets up to 100% of astrocytes in the striatum.
source: This method targeted up to 100% of astrocytes in the striatum (tdTomato expression in 92 ± 10% of glutamine synthetase+, S100+ cells; mean ± S.D.; n = 6 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the efficiency of the Cx30-CreER system.

claim: Cx30-CreER mice target neural stem cells in the SVZ, but no other brain cell types.
source: These mice also target neural stem cells in the SVZ, but no other brain cell types (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Rbpj deletion in healthy mice constitutes a single, precisely timed trigger throughout the brain.
source: Rbpj deletion in healthy mice was chosen as the means by which to activate the neurogenic program of astrocytes. That is because (1) it constitutes a single, precisely timed trigger throughout the brain, (2) it mimics the endogenous stimulus of reduced Notch signaling by which stroke induces neurogenesis by astrocytes (Magnusson et al., 2014), and (3) it does not induce potentially confounding cellular processes like reactive gliosis or cell death.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental approach.

claim: Rbpj deletion mimics the endogenous stimulus of reduced Notch signaling by which stroke induces neurogenesis by astrocytes.
source: it mimics the endogenous stimulus of reduced Notch signaling by which stroke induces neurogenesis by astrocytes (Magnusson et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Rbpj deletion does not induce potentially confounding cellular processes like reactive gliosis or cell death.
source: it does not induce potentially confounding cellular processes like reactive gliosis or cell death.
evidence: This is an observation from the study justifying the experimental approach.

claim: The AAV-Cre dataset contained a somewhat higher proportion of transit-amplifying cells than the Cx30-CreER dataset.
source: The AAV-Cre dataset contained a somewhat higher proportion of transit-amplifying cells than the Cx30-CreER dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f), likely because the AAV-Cre dataset only contained cells from 5 weeks after Rbpj-KO, near the peak of transit-amplifying divisions (Magnusson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two datasets with an explanation based on timing.
